cards.q: Why can a variadic function not find out how many arguments it received?
cards.a: C passes no count or type information; the function must be told through a count, a sentinel or a format.

cards.q: What type should `va_arg` use for an argument that was passed as a `float`?
cards.a: `double`, because floats are promoted to double when passed through `...`.

cards.q: Why is `struct { char a; double b; char c; }` bigger than 10 bytes?
cards.a: Padding: `b` must start at a multiple of 8, and the struct's size is rounded up to its alignment so arrays of it stay aligned.
cards.lessonTitle: Struct Layout, Alignment and Bit Fields

cards.q: Why are bit fields a poor choice for a file format?
cards.a: The order and packing of the bits inside the integer are up to the compiler, so another compiler may read them differently.
cards.lessonTitle: Struct Layout, Alignment and Bit Fields

cards.q: In `int a[6] = { [4] = 9 };`, what are the other elements?
cards.a: 0: elements not mentioned in an initializer are zero.

cards.q: When is a `_Static_assert` checked?
cards.a: While compiling: a false condition stops the build with its message.

cards.q: Why copy `errno` straight after the failing call?
cards.a: The next library call, even a successful one like `printf`, may change it.

cards.q: Why are the cleanup labels in reverse order of acquiring?
cards.a: A failure at step N jumps to the label that releases what steps before N acquired, and falls through the rest in reverse order.

cards.q: Why does giving each thread its own result slot avoid locking?
cards.a: No two threads write the same memory, so there is no data race; the main thread reads the slots only after joining.

cards.q: Why must `cnd_wait` be called in a loop?
cards.a: A thread can wake without the condition being true (a spurious wake-up, or another thread got there first), so it must check again.

cards.q: What does `snprintf(NULL, 0, fmt, ...)` return?
cards.a: The number of characters the full output would have (not counting the zero), without writing anything.

cards.q: Why does the capacity double instead of growing by the amount needed?
cards.a: So the number of reallocations stays small and appending stays O(1) on average, instead of copying everything on every append.

cards.q: Why cast a `void *` to `unsigned char *` before adding an offset?
cards.a: Arithmetic needs a pointed-to size; `unsigned char` is one byte, so the offset counts bytes.

cards.q: What must be true of an array before `bsearch` can search it?
cards.a: It must be sorted with the same comparison function that `bsearch` is given.

cards.q: What does `t.tm_mon == 0` mean?
cards.a: January: months in `struct tm` count from 0.

cards.q: How can `mktime` help with "30 days after this date"?
cards.a: Add 30 to `tm_mday` and call `mktime`; it normalises the date into the right month and year.

cards.q: Why should error messages go to `stderr`?
cards.a: So redirecting or piping the output only carries the real results, and errors still reach the person.

cards.q: What does `--` on a command line mean?
cards.a: The end of the options: everything after it is taken as a file name or argument, even if it starts with `-`.

cards.q: Why is `if (a + b < a)` a broken overflow test for `int`?
cards.a: The overflow has already happened, and signed overflow is undefined, so the compiler may assume it cannot happen and remove the test.

cards.q: What happens to `-1` in `strlen(s) > -1`?
cards.a: It is converted to `size_t`, becoming the largest possible value, so the comparison is always false.

cards.q: Why does `rand() % n` favour small numbers?
cards.a: When `RAND_MAX + 1` is not a multiple of `n`, the last incomplete group of values maps only onto the smallest results.

cards.q: Why keep a generator's state in a struct instead of a global?
cards.a: Each part of the program (or each thread) can have its own repeatable stream, and nothing else disturbs it.
